context: rotating machinery & HV energisation · long back-end commissioning chain

brief.intro: New to this project type? A power generation or utility plant (gas, steam, combined-cycle, or a large renewable/BESS interconnection) exists to deliver electricity to the grid — everything else is in service of that. The turbine-generator (rotating machinery) and the high-voltage electrical system dominate the schedule; the boiler or HRSG civil-mechanical scope is large but is not where the real risk sits. The risk sits in a long, tightly sequenced commissioning chain at the back end: steam blow, then first fire, then first synchronisation to the grid, then a reliability run — each step gates the next, and re-tests are common. The earthing grid and HV protection/energisation are first-class systems in their own right, not secondary electrical items.

a high-velocity steam flush of the piping to clean out debris before the turbine is allowed to see steam.

Balance of Plant — the supporting systems (cooling water, water treatment, fuel handling) around the main turbine/boiler train.
the control systems that regulate the generator's voltage and the turbine's speed.
the outdoor high-voltage equipment — breakers, transformers, busbars — that connects the plant to the grid.
a sustained trial-operation period proving the plant holds its output before commercial handover.

must_get_right: The driving path is procurement of the turbine-generator, boiler/HRSG and main transformer — not the structure; order them first and track them as milestones.
Protect the commissioning chain end to end — steam blow → first fire → first sync → reliability run; each step gates the next and re-tests are common.
Earthing grid and HV protection/energisation are safety-critical and must be proven before any energisation step, not treated as routine electrical fit-out.
Cooling water and BOP systems must be ready ahead of first fire — they are enabling systems, not finishing items.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week; mechanical erection of the turbine-generator and boiler/HRSG moves to two shifts at peak; commissioning runs a continuous (24-hour) calendar once steam blow begins through to first synchronisation and the reliability run.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs long-lead procurement (turbine-generator, boiler/HRSG, main transformer) → heavy foundations → mechanical erection → HV switchyard & earthing → steam blow → first fire → first synchronisation to the grid → reliability run. This back-end commissioning chain, not the civil structure, is the true critical path.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen; grid-interconnection and environmental approvals are obtained per phase gate; a single mobilisation; and the grid operator has confirmed the synchronisation window in advance. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy lifts (turbine-generator modules, boiler drums, transformers) require large crane windows and clear haul routes; first synchronisation depends on a grid-outage or interconnection window controlled by the utility/grid operator; skilled commissioning engineers are shared across the turbine, boiler and electrical disciplines and are a resource constraint late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead slippage on the turbine-generator, boiler/HRSG or main transformer; steam-blow re-runs; and grid-synchronisation scheduling delays outside the contractor's control. Schedule contingency is held immediately before steam blow and before first synchronisation rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
